finding.claim: POST /settings/email uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing, account-modifying endpoint. It is likely a decorator mix-up, since the sibling /settings/password route uses login_required. The impact depends on set_email's real implementation, which is a stub here. A None uid could update a row with a NULL user id, or a shared or guest record, or raise an error. It could also enable account takeover through email change and password reset if set_email handles None badly. No CSRF protection is visible either.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated remote client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which changes the account email

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when there is no session, and never aborts
set_email(None, 'new@example.org') is called without any auth check
For comparison, /settings/password uses @login_required, which aborts 401 at line 12

finding.guards_checked: Checked for login_required (absent on this route), any in-handler check of g.uid (none), any other before_request hook or auth middleware (none in the file), and CSRF protection (none visible). set_email is a stub, so downstream validation of uid could not be checked.

verdict.guard_found: none: login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid and never aborts; no in-handler check, no before_request hook, no CSRF protection
